summaries.example: Imagine a spinning arrow that can point in several ways. Before you look, quantum mechanics gives possible results and the chances of each result. A modal interpretation says the arrow really has one definite result when the situation calls for it, but the ordinary quantum state does not always tell us which result it already has. The quantum state keeps changing smoothly; it does not suddenly jump because someone looks.
summaries.summary: Modal interpretations are a family of proposals about what quantum mechanics means. They keep the quantum state evolving continuously according to the usual rule, rather than making it collapse whenever a measurement happens. But they add an account of definite properties: things such as a detector’s pointer can have one actual value even when the quantum state is a mixture or superposition of possibilities. The quantum state tells us which properties may be definite and gives probabilities for them. Different modal proposals choose these properties in different ways. Some use mathematical decompositions of the state, some give a special role to the Hamiltonian, and perspectival versions describe properties relative to another physical system. These ideas aim to explain measurements in one world, while accepting that quantum events are fundamentally probabilistic. Decoherence, caused by interaction with an environment, can make the properties selected for a large measuring device closely resemble the properties we observe. The approach remains an active research program with open questions about property choices, time, probability, and relativity.
key_ideas: Modal interpretations are a family of ways to understand quantum mechanics, not just one single theory.
They keep the usual smooth quantum evolution and do not add a collapse during measurement.
A quantum state gives possible properties and their probabilities, while a value state describes which properties are definite.
Different modal interpretations use different rules for choosing the definite properties.
Some versions say properties belong to one system alone; perspectival versions say properties can depend on another system’s viewpoint.
Decoherence can help explain why measuring devices have stable-looking results, although some technical questions remain.
summaries.why_it_matters: Quantum mechanics predicts experiments extremely well, but its mathematical state can describe several possible results at once. Modal interpretations ask how one real world can contain definite things without adding a sudden collapse. They offer a way to discuss actual properties and probabilities while keeping the usual quantum evolution. Comparing their different proposals also shows why ideas such as viewpoint, measurement, and the connection between parts and wholes matter in science.

important_terms.definition: A way of explaining what the mathematical rules of quantum mechanics say about reality.
A possible physical feature with one definite value, such as a pointer pointing left or right.
A description of what may happen and how likely each possibility is.
The actual definite properties a system has at a particular time.
A proposed sudden jump in the quantum state during measurement. Modal interpretations leave this jump out.
A process in which many small possibilities become separated enough that ordinary large objects look definite.

questions_to_think_about: If a theory gives chances for several results, does it also need to say which result is actual?
Should a property belong to an object by itself, or can it depend on its relation to another object?
Why might a measuring device need a definite pointer position?
What problems could appear if different ways of dividing a larger system give different properties?

summaries.example: Consider a qubit measured by a pointer. Unitary quantum mechanics can describe the interaction as producing an entangled state in which each possible qubit result is correlated with a different pointer position. A modal interpretation does not replace this evolution with collapse. Instead, an actualization rule selects a set of commuting observables that can have definite values, and the state supplies probabilities for the alternatives. In a biorthogonal or spectral version, the correlations in the joint state can select the qubit basis and pointer basis. summaries.summary: Modal interpretations form a broad family of realist, non-collapse interpretations of quantum mechanics. Their central move is to retain the standard unitary evolution of the quantum state while distinguishing that dynamical state from a value state describing which observables are actually definite. The dynamical state supplies a structured set of possibilities and Born probabilities; it need not itself be an eigenstate of every observable whose value is definite. Since the Kochen-Specker theorem rules out assigning compatible values to all observables at once, a modal interpretation must specify an actualization rule and a preferred context of definite-valued observables. The biorthogonal-decomposition and spectral-decomposition approaches extract this context from the state, while the atomic modal approach uses a preferred factorization and the modal-Hamiltonian approach uses the Hamiltonian and its symmetries. Perspectival modal interpretations instead treat properties as relative to reference systems, offering a relational treatment of situations such as EPR correlations. These proposals can account for unique-looking outcomes without fundamental collapse, but they face questions about how properties compose between systems, how actual properties evolve, and how non-ideal measurements work. Decoherence often brings the selected macroscopic properties close to ordinary pointer variables, though continuous and infinite-dimensional cases remain difficult. Modal interpretations therefore offer a flexible research program rather than a single settled solution.
key_ideas: Modal interpretations accept universal, unitary quantum mechanics and reject the projection postulate as a fundamental measurement rule.
They distinguish the dynamical state from the value state: the former encodes possibilities and probabilities, while the latter represents actual definite properties.
Because the Kochen-Specker theorem blocks simultaneous definite values for all observables, each modal theory needs an actualization rule selecting a compatible subset.

BDMI and SDMI derive the preferred context from biorthogonal or spectral decompositions; AMI introduces a preferred factorization into atomic systems; MHI gives the Hamiltonian a determining role; PMI makes properties perspectival.
The measurement problem is addressed without collapse or many worlds, but non-ideal measurements, degeneracy, property composition, dynamics, and decoherence create substantial challenges.
Modal interpretations are fundamentally probabilistic, yet they disagree about whether probabilities express ignorance of actual values, objective propensities, or both.
summaries.why_it_matters: The measurement problem arises from tension among three ideas: the quantum state may be complete, it evolves linearly, and measurements have unique outcomes. Modal interpretations retain linear evolution and unique outcomes by denying that the quantum state alone fixes every actual property. Their proposals clarify what a realist quantum theory might say about one world, probability, and measurement without invoking collapse or multiple worlds. At the same time, their disagreements expose deep issues about context, subsystem identity, relationality, determinism, and the possible extension of quantum interpretations to relativity and quantum field theory.

important_terms.definition: A family of interpretations that keeps unitary quantum evolution but adds an account of definite properties, possible values, and their probabilities.
The quantum state used in the dynamical equations; it determines possibilities and probabilities but need not list every actual property.
A description of the definite-valued observables that are actual at a particular time.
The principle that a system has a sharp value exactly when its quantum state is the matching eigenstate; modal views reject the ‘only if’ direction.
A rule that selects which observables may possess definite values from the state, or from the state plus a preferred observable.
A non-collapse approach in which the quantum state evolves unitarily rather than undergoing a measurement-induced jump.
A choice of compatible, definite-valued observables that forms the setting in which ordinary probabilities can be defined.
The loss of observable interference through interaction with an environment, often making macroscopic alternatives effectively distinct.

questions_to_think_about: Does denying that the quantum state fixes every actual property amount to incompleteness, or can it be a complete description of a fundamentally probabilistic world?
If a property of a subsystem and a mathematically related property of the composite system give different assignments, should that count as a contradiction?
Can decoherence robustly select the properties required for realistic measuring devices, especially when infinitely many degrees of freedom are involved?
Would a relational account of properties help with nonlocal-looking correlations and with compatibility between quantum theory and relativity?
How much additional structure should an interpretation provide: only single-time probabilities, or also a dynamics connecting actual properties across time?

summaries.example: Think of a quantum system and a measuring device as two dancers whose movements become linked. After they interact, one dance pattern matches one pointer position, and another pattern matches a different position. The ordinary quantum equation describes the linking smoothly; it does not include a special magic jump when someone watches. A modal interpretation adds a rule saying which features can be definite. One version may use the pattern of links in the combined system. Another may say the features depend on which physical system is used as a reference. The environment can also help make the pointer’s possible positions behave like separate, stable choices.
summaries.summary: Modal interpretations are a group of proposals about how to understand quantum mechanics as a theory of one real world. They remove the projection or collapse postulate, so the quantum state always follows the ordinary smooth evolution described by the Schrödinger equation. To explain definite outcomes, they distinguish the dynamical state from the value state. The dynamical state describes which properties are possible and gives their probabilities. The value state describes the properties that are actually definite at that time. A central challenge is deciding which properties can be definite. The Kochen-Specker theorem shows that all physical quantities cannot receive compatible sharp values simultaneously, so each modal interpretation needs an actualization rule. Some approaches use a mathematical decomposition of the state, others use a preferred observable such as the Hamiltonian, and perspectival approaches define properties relative to reference systems. The interpretations also differ over whether probability represents limited knowledge of an actual value or a deeper tendency for a possibility to become actual. They can describe measurements without collapse, but questions remain about imperfect measurements, changing properties, the relation between wholes and parts, and the role of decoherence.
key_ideas: The modal approach now includes several related interpretations rather than one uniform theory.
It keeps quantum evolution continuous and treats measurements as ordinary physical interactions.
A system can have a definite property even when its dynamical state is not the corresponding eigenstate.
The Kochen-Specker theorem means that no interpretation can simply assign sharp values to every quantity at once while preserving all the usual relations.
Different proposals disagree about how to choose definite properties: from the quantum state, from a preferred observable, from a preferred factorization, or relative to a reference system.
Decoherence may explain why the properties selected for a macroscopic apparatus are close to its familiar pointer positions, but it does not remove every open problem.
summaries.why_it_matters: Quantum mechanics is successful but difficult to interpret because its equations can describe several possible outcomes while experiments seem to produce one result. Modal interpretations try to keep the equations’ continuous evolution and still describe definite properties in a single world. Studying them helps us see that interpreting a scientific theory involves more than calculating predictions: it also involves deciding what counts as a real property, how probability works, and whether descriptions depend on physical relationships.

important_terms.definition: A family of interpretations that explains quantum mechanics using definite properties and probabilities without a fundamental collapse.
The quantum description that changes according to the Schrödinger equation and lists possible properties with their chances.
The set of properties that are actually definite for a system at a given moment.
The proposed sudden change of the quantum state during a measurement; modal interpretations do not treat it as fundamental.
A rule for choosing which observables are allowed to have definite values.
A set of compatible properties used as the framework for assigning ordinary probabilities.
A way quantum systems can lose visible interference through interaction with their surroundings, helping large objects look classical.
The idea that a system’s properties may be defined relative to another system rather than absolutely by itself.

questions_to_think_about: Is a theory incomplete if it gives probabilities for actual values but does not determine those values in advance?
When two systems are parts of a larger system, should their properties always combine into the larger system’s properties?
Could two different observers’ descriptions of one quantum object both be objective if they are relative to different systems?
Why might a theory need rules about how definite properties change over time, rather than only rules for one instant?
